intro: The Talmud is full of stories about rabbis. A rabbi is a Jewish teacher. In this unit you will meet three of them: Hillel, Honi, and Akiva. They lived about 2,000 years ago. Jewish tradition still tells their stories today.

Each story has a picture in it. A man hops on one foot. An old man plants a tree. Water drips on a stone. You will read the stories and talk about them. Then you will find the big idea inside each one.

By the end, you will be able to tell each story in your own words. You will know what Hillel said on one foot. You will know why the old man planted his tree. And you will know how Akiva learned to read.
bigQuestion: What do the rabbis' stories teach about being kind, giving, and learning?

timeline.t: Meet Hillel and Shammai, two rabbis who often disagreed.
A man asks to learn the whole Torah on one foot, and Shammai sends him away.
Hillel gives one short rule: what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend.
A man tries to make Hillel angry and cannot.
Honi meets an old man planting a carob tree for his grandchildren.
Honi sleeps seventy years and sees the tree giving fruit.
Akiva the shepherd sees water wearing a hole in a stone.
Akiva starts to learn at forty and becomes a great rabbi.
We compare the stories and find what they teach.

words.d: a Jewish teacher; the Talmud is full of rabbis asking and answering questions
the first five books of the Bible, kept as a scroll
a patient rabbi who gave one short rule to a man standing on one foot
a strict rabbi who lived at the same time as Hillel and often disagreed with him
something you would hate to have done to you
a Jewish teacher who met an old man planting a carob tree
a famous rabbi who began as a shepherd and started learning at about forty
able to stay calm and wait, even when something is hard

write.prompt: Pick one story: Hillel on one foot (Shabbat 31a), Honi and the carob tree (Ta'anit 23a), or Akiva and the water (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 6). Draw or tell the story. Then say what Jewish tradition teaches from it.

title: Rabbis Who Told Stories

chapters.title: Hillel on One Foot
chapters.bigQuestion: What did Hillel teach a man who could only stand on one foot?

story.title: The Man Who Hopped
story.kicker: A man hops on one foot and asks for the whole Torah before he falls over.
paragraphs: Long ago, about 2,000 years ago, a man came to a teacher named Shammai. The man had a strange idea. He said, "Teach me the whole Torah. Teach it while I stand on one foot." Then he lifted one foot and began to hop.
Shammai was a builder. He held a builder's stick in his hand. The Talmud says Shammai got upset. The Torah is very long! Nobody can learn it that fast. Shammai pushed the man away with his stick.
The man did not give up. He hopped to another teacher named Hillel. He asked the same thing. "Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot." Hillel did not get upset. He thought for a moment.

Then Hillel said something short. "What is hateful to you, do not do to your friend. That is the whole Torah. The rest explains it. Go and learn." The man put his foot down. He had his answer. Now he wanted to learn more.
story.think: Why do you think Hillel gave a short answer instead of a long one?

lessons.title: Who Was Hillel?
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel was a rabbi who lived about 2,000 years ago and was known for being patient.
reading: A *rabbi* is a Jewish teacher. Hillel was a rabbi. He lived about 2,000 years ago. He lived in the land of Israel. Jewish tradition says he came from Babylonia. That is far to the east.
The Talmud tells many stories about Hillel. In the stories, Hillel stays calm. He is kind to people who ask questions. He is kind even when they are rude.
Hillel had many students. Jewish tradition calls them the House of Hillel. They studied his ideas for a long time after he died.

words.d: a Jewish teacher; the Talmud is full of rabbis asking and answering questions
a rabbi who lived about 2,000 years ago, known in the Talmud for being patient and kind

look.title: Picture a Patient Teacher
look.text: Look at a teacher sitting on a low bench. A child runs up and asks a question. Then another child asks. Then another. The teacher does not sigh. The teacher smiles and answers each one. The Talmud says Hillel was like this.
look.prompt: How can you tell when a teacher is being patient?

check.q: What is a rabbi?
check.why: A rabbi is a Jewish teacher. The Talmud is full of rabbis.

check.q: About how long ago did Hillel live?
check.why: Hillel lived about 2,000 years ago in the land of Israel.

check.q: In the Talmud's stories, how does Hillel act?
check.why: The Talmud shows Hillel staying calm and kind, even with rude people.

lessons.title: Who Was Shammai?
lessons.mainIdea: Shammai was a rabbi who lived at the same time as Hillel, and the two often disagreed.
reading: *Shammai* was a rabbi too. He lived at the same time as Hillel. The Talmud says he was a builder. He was strict. He liked rules to be clear and firm.
Hillel and Shammai often did not agree. Their students did not agree either. The Talmud writes down both sides. It does not throw one side away.
Jewish tradition still tells about both teachers. Both cared about the Torah. They just saw things in different ways. The Talmud says that is all right.

words.d: a rabbi who lived at the same time as Hillel; the Talmud says he was strict and often disagreed with Hillel
to think differently from someone about something

look.title: Two Ways to Answer
look.text: Two kids get the same question: "Can I borrow your crayon?" One says, "Yes, but give it right back." The other says, "Yes, keep it as long as you need." Both are trying to be fair. They just think about it differently.
look.prompt: Can two people both be fair and still disagree? How?

check.q: What job does the Talmud say Shammai had?
check.why: The Talmud says Shammai was a builder and held a builder's stick.

check.q: What did the Talmud do with the ideas of Hillel and Shammai?
check.why: The Talmud keeps both sides of a disagreement. It does not throw one away.

check.q: When did Shammai live?
choices: at the same time as Hillel
check.why: Shammai and Hillel were rabbis at the same time, about 2,000 years ago.

lessons.title: A Strange Request
lessons.mainIdea: A man asked to learn the whole Torah while standing on one foot, and Shammai sent him away.
reading: The *Torah* is the first five books of the Bible. It is very long. Jewish people read it a little each week. It takes a whole year to read it all.
The Talmud tells about a man. He wanted to learn the whole Torah fast. He said he would stand on one foot. Teach me before I fall over, he said.
The man asked Shammai first. Shammai thought the question was silly. He sent the man away. The Talmud says he used his builder's stick.

words.d: the first five books of the Bible, kept as a scroll and read by Jewish people each week

look.title: The Talmud Tells the Story
look.text: The Talmud tells it this way. A man came to Shammai and said: Make me Jewish, but teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring stick he was holding.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a, retold in simple words (compare Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: Why do you think Shammai thought the question was silly?

check.q: What is the Torah?
choices: the first five books of the Bible
check.why: The Torah is the first five books of the Bible. It is very long.

check.q: What did the man want?
choices: to learn the whole Torah fast
check.why: The man wanted to learn the whole Torah while standing on one foot.

check.q: What did Shammai do?
choices: He taught the man all day.
He stood on one foot too.
check.why: The Talmud says Shammai sent the man away with his builder's stick.

lessons.title: Hillel's Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel said: what is hateful to you, do not do to another; the rest is explanation, go and learn.
reading: The man hopped to Hillel. He asked the same thing. Hillel did not send him away. Hillel gave him one short rule.
The rule was this. What is *hateful* to you, do not do to your friend. Hateful means something you would hate. If you hate being teased, do not tease.
Then Hillel said more. That is the whole Torah, he said. The rest explains it. Go and learn. The Talmud says the man went and learned.

words.d: something you would hate to have done to you
to tell more about something so it makes sense

look.title: Hillel's Short Rule
look.text: The Talmud says Hillel told the man: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah. The rest is its explanation. Go and learn it.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a, retold in simple words (compare Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: Say Hillel's rule in your own words. What would it mean at recess?

check.q: What did Hillel do when the man asked?
choices: He gave him one short rule.
check.why: Hillel gave the man one short rule instead of sending him away.

check.q: What does hateful mean?
check.why: Hateful means something you would hate to have done to you.

check.q: What did Hillel say the rest of the Torah does?
check.why: Hillel said the rest of the Torah explains the rule. Go and learn it.

lessons.title: Hillel Stays Calm
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud shows Hillel staying patient even when people try to make him angry.
reading: The Talmud tells another story about Hillel. Two men made a bet. One said he could make Hillel angry. He went to Hillel's house on a busy day.
The man knocked and asked silly questions. Why do some people have round heads? Why do some people have weak eyes? Hillel came out each time. He answered kindly.
The man could not make Hillel angry. He lost his bet. Being *patient* means staying calm when it is hard. The Talmud holds up Hillel as patient.

words.d: able to stay calm and wait, even when something is hard or slow

look.title: The Bet
look.text: The Talmud tells that a man bet a large sum that he could make Hillel angry. He kept calling Hillel out of his house with silly questions. Each time Hillel came, wrapped himself in his cloak, and said, My son, what do you want? At the end the man said, You made me lose my bet. Hillel answered that it was better to lose the money than for Hillel to lose his temper.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a, retold in simple words (compare Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: What did Hillel say was worth more than money?

check.q: What did the man try to do?
check.why: The man bet that he could make Hillel angry. He lost.

check.q: What does patient mean?
check.why: Patient means staying calm even when something is hard or slow.

check.q: How did Hillel answer the silly questions?
check.why: The Talmud says Hillel came out each time and answered kindly.

lessons.title: Go and Learn
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel's rule starts with kindness, and learning is how you find out the rest.
reading: Hillel's rule is short. You can say it on one foot. But Hillel did not stop there. He said, go and *learn*. One rule is a start, not the end.
Many people know a rule like Hillel's. Some call it the Golden Rule. Jewish tradition points to a verse in the Torah too: love your neighbor as yourself. That verse is in Leviticus.
Kindness comes first in Hillel's rule. Learning comes next. This course will read many rules the rabbis made. Many of them are about being *kind*.

words.d: to find out something new by reading, asking, or trying
caring about how other people feel and helping them

look.title: A Verse in the Torah
look.text: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
look.prompt: How is this verse like Hillel's rule? How is it different?

check.q: What did Hillel tell the man to do after the rule?
check.why: Hillel said the rest explains the rule, so go and learn.

check.q: Which book of the Torah says to love your neighbor?
check.why: The verse is in Leviticus 19:18. The Talmud is not part of the Torah.

check.q: What comes first in Hillel's rule?
check.why: Hillel's rule starts with kindness: do not do to others what you would hate.

choices: two rabbis who lived about 2,000 years ago
review.why: Hillel and Shammai were two rabbis, Jewish teachers, who lived about 2,000 years ago.

review.q: What did the man ask the teachers to do?
choices: teach the whole Torah while he stood on one foot
review.why: He asked to learn the whole Torah while standing on one foot.

review.q: Which teacher sent the man away?
review.why: The Talmud says Shammai pushed the man away with his builder's stick.

choices: What is hateful to you, do not do to your friend.
review.why: Hillel said: what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend.

review.q: Where is the story of Hillel and the man on one foot found?
review.why: The story is in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page 31a.

review.q: What does the Talmud say about Hillel's patience?
choices: He got angry at silly questions.
A man could not make him angry, even with silly questions.
review.why: A man bet he could make Hillel angry and lost. Hillel stayed patient.

chapters.title: Honi and the Carob Tree, Akiva and the Water
chapters.bigQuestion: What can a tree and a drip of water teach about learning and giving?

story.title: A Tree for Someone Else
story.kicker: An old man plants a tree he will never eat from, and a passerby cannot understand why.
paragraphs: One day a man named Honi was walking down a road. He saw an old man digging a hole. The old man put a small tree in the hole. It was a carob tree. Honi stopped to watch.
Honi asked a question. "How long until this tree gives fruit?" The old man said, "Seventy years." Honi was surprised. Seventy years is a very long time. The old man would not live that long.

"Then why plant it?" Honi asked. "You will never eat from it." The old man smiled. He said, "When I was born, there were carob trees. My grandparents planted them for me. So I plant this tree for my grandchildren."
Honi sat down to think about that. The Talmud says he fell asleep. And the story gets even stranger. But that part is for the next lesson.
story.think: Have you ever done something nice for a person you will never meet? What was it?

lessons.title: A Man Plants a Tree
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells how Honi met an old man planting a carob tree for his grandchildren.
reading: *Honi* was a Jewish teacher. He lived about 2,000 years ago in the land of Israel. Jewish tradition remembers him for praying for rain. The Talmud tells stories about him.
In one story, Honi saw an old man plant a *carob* tree. A carob tree grows sweet brown pods. But it takes a long time to grow. The old man said: seventy years.
Honi asked why plant it. The old man said his grandparents planted trees for him. So he would plant for his grandchildren. He was planting for people not born yet.

words.d: a Jewish teacher from about 2,000 years ago; the Talmud tells how he met a man planting a carob tree
a tree that grows sweet brown pods; the Talmud says it takes seventy years to give fruit

look.title: The Talmud Tells It
look.text: The Talmud says Honi saw a man planting a carob tree and asked how many years until it would bear fruit. The man said seventy years. Honi asked if he was sure he would live seventy years. The man answered that he found carob trees in the world when he was born; as his ancestors planted for him, he was planting for his descendants.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a, retold in simple words (compare Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: Who did the old man say planted trees for him?

check.q: What kind of tree did the old man plant?
check.why: The Talmud says the old man planted a carob tree.

check.q: How long did the old man say the tree would take?
check.why: The old man said the carob tree would give fruit in seventy years.

check.q: Who was the old man planting the tree for?
check.why: He said he was planting for his grandchildren, as his grandparents had planted for him.

lessons.title: Seventy Years
lessons.mainIdea: In the Talmud's story, Honi sleeps seventy years and wakes to see the tree giving fruit.
reading: The story goes on. Honi sat down to eat. He fell asleep. Rocks hid him from sight. The Talmud says he slept for *seventy* years!
When Honi woke up, he saw a man picking carobs. It was the same tree. Honi asked, "Did you plant this?" The man said, "No. My grandfather did."
The old man's plan had worked. His grandchild was eating the fruit. Jewish tradition tells this story to teach about giving to the future.

words.d: the number 70; in the story, how long a carob tree takes and how long Honi slept

look.title: Numbers in the Stories
rows: Years for the carob tree to give fruit
Years Honi slept in the story
Akiva's age when he started to learn
Years Akiva studied away from home
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a; Ketubot 62b–63a; Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 6
look.prompt: Which two numbers are the same? Why do you think the story uses the same number twice?

check.q: What happened to Honi after he sat down?
check.why: The Talmud says Honi fell asleep and slept for seventy years.

check.q: Who was picking carobs when Honi woke up?
check.why: The man said his grandfather had planted the tree. He was the grandchild.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition use this story to teach?
check.why: The story is told to teach about planting for people who come after us.

lessons.title: The Shepherd
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Akiva started as a shepherd who could not read, and he began to learn as a grown-up.
reading: Rabbi *Akiva* became one of the most famous rabbis in the Talmud. But he did not start as a rabbi. He started as a *shepherd*. A shepherd takes care of sheep.
Akiva was poor. He could not read. He worked for a rich man. The Talmud says the rich man's daughter saw that Akiva was good and humble. She married him.
She told Akiva to go and study. Jewish tradition says he was about forty years old. He had to learn the alphabet, like a small child. He did it anyway.

words.d: a famous rabbi in the Talmud who began as a shepherd and started learning as a grown-up
a person who takes care of sheep

look.title: Starting Late
look.text: Look at a grown man sitting on a small bench. Around him are little children. They are all learning the alphabet. The man is much older than everyone else. He holds his slate and says the letters out loud, one by one. He does not look ashamed. He looks like he wants to learn.
look.prompt: How might Akiva have felt learning with little children? What might have helped him keep going?

check.q: What was Akiva's first job?
check.why: The Talmud says Akiva was a shepherd before he learned to read.

check.q: About how old was Akiva when he began to learn?
check.why: Jewish tradition says Akiva was about forty when he began to study.

check.q: Who told Akiva to go and study?
check.why: The Talmud says his wife told him to go and learn Torah.

lessons.title: Water and Stone
lessons.mainIdea: Akiva saw water wearing a hole in a stone and decided learning could shape him too.
reading: Jewish tradition tells how Akiva got the courage to learn. One day he stood by a well. He saw a stone with a hole in it. Water dripped on the stone.
Akiva asked, "Who made this hole?" People said the water did. It fell drip by drip, day after day. Slowly, it wore a hole in the hard stone.
Akiva thought about that. Water is soft. Stone is hard. But water won. He said: if water can shape stone, then learning can shape me. He began to *study*.

words.d: to spend time learning something, a little at a time

look.title: The Drip That Won
look.text: An old rabbinic book tells that Akiva, at forty years old, had not yet learned anything. He stood by a well and saw a stone worn away. He asked who had hollowed it out, and was told the water had done it, drop by drop. He said to himself: if soft water can carve hard stone, then words of Torah, which are hard, can surely carve my heart, which is flesh.
look.cite: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 6, retold in simple words
look.prompt: What did Akiva decide when he saw the hole in the stone?

check.q: What made the hole in the stone?
check.why: The water dripped on the stone day after day and wore a hole in it.

check.q: What did Akiva decide?
choices: Learning could shape him, a little at a time.
He was too old to learn.
check.why: Akiva said that if water can shape stone, learning can shape him.

check.q: Which book tells the water and stone story?
check.why: The story is in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an old rabbinic book, chapter 6.

lessons.title: Planting for Others
lessons.mainIdea: The carob tree story teaches about giving to people who will come after us.
reading: Think about the old man again. He worked hard. He dug a hole and planted a tree. He knew he would never taste the fruit. He did it anyway.
Jewish tradition calls this kind of giving a gift to the *future*. The future is the time that has not come yet. You can help people you will never meet.
Kids can plant for the future too. You can plant a real tree. You can leave a room clean for the next class. You can teach a younger kid a game.

words.d: the time that has not come yet; tomorrow, next year, and long after

look.title: A Gift You Will Not See
look.text: Look at a class planting little trees on the edge of a playground in Chicago. The trees are only as tall as the kids. In many years, they will be tall and shady. The kids who planted them will be grown up and gone. New kids will sit in the shade.
look.prompt: What is one thing you could do this week for someone who comes after you?

check.q: What does future mean?
choices: the time that has not come yet
check.why: The future is the time that has not come yet.

check.q: Why is the old man's tree a gift to the future?
choices: Other people will eat the fruit after him.
The tree grew in one day.
check.why: The old man planted so that his grandchildren would eat from the tree.

check.q: Which is a way a kid can plant for the future?
choices: leaving a room clean for the next class
check.why: Leaving a room clean helps the people who come after you.

lessons.title: Never Too Late
lessons.mainIdea: Akiva's story teaches that it is never too late to learn, and that small steps add up.
reading: Akiva began learning at about forty. The Talmud says he studied for many years. He became a great rabbi. Many students came to learn from him.
The Talmud tells stories of the rabbis to teach. Akiva's story teaches two things. It is *never too late* to learn. And little steps add up, like drips of water.
The Talmud is full of rabbis like Hillel, Honi, and Akiva. Their stories are still told today. In this course, you will meet many more of them.

words.d: you can always start; a person can learn at any age

look.title: Two Stories, One Idea
look.text: Story one: an old man plants a tree for seventy years from now. Story two: a grown man learns his letters, one drip at a time. In both stories, something big happens slowly. In both, a person keeps going without seeing the end.
look.prompt: What do the two stories have in common? What is different?

check.q: What does Akiva's story teach?
choices: It is never too late to learn.
check.why: Jewish tradition tells Akiva's story to show that learning can start at any age.

check.q: What did Akiva become?
choices: a great rabbi with many students
check.why: The Talmud says Akiva became a great rabbi with many students.

check.q: How do little steps in learning work, like the water?
check.why: Like drips of water on stone, small steps in learning add up over time.

review.q: Who saw an old man planting a carob tree?
review.why: The Talmud, in Ta'anit 23a, says Honi saw the old man planting the tree.

review.q: Why did the old man plant a tree he would never eat from?
choices: He was planting for his grandchildren.
He did not know it was slow.
review.why: He said his grandparents planted for him, so he planted for his grandchildren.

review.q: How long did the Talmud say Honi slept?
review.why: In the story Honi sleeps seventy years and wakes to see the tree giving fruit.

review.q: What was Akiva before he was a rabbi?
choices: a shepherd who could not read
review.why: The Talmud says Akiva was a poor shepherd who had not learned to read.

review.q: What did Akiva see that made him want to learn?
choices: water wearing a hole in a stone
review.why: Akiva saw water dripping on a stone and decided learning could shape him.

review.q: Which story tells that it is never too late to learn?
review.why: Akiva began learning at about forty and became a great rabbi.
